title: Effect of precipitants during the preparation of Cu-ZnO-Al2O3/Zr-ferrierite catalyst on the DME synthesis from syngas
journalName: Journal of Industrial and Engineering Chemistry
abstract: The synthesis of dimethyl ether (DME) from biomass-derived model synthesis gas has been investigated on Cu-ZnO-Al2O3/Zr-ferrierite bifunctional catalysts. The catalysts are prepared by co-precipitation–impregnation method using Na2CO3, K2CO3 and (NH4)2CO3 as the precipitants. The catalytic activity tests reveal that the best yield of DME can be obtained on the catalyst precipitated by using (NH4)2CO3. Detailed characterization studies conducted on the catalysts to measure their properties such as surface area, acidity by temperature-programmed desorption of ammonia (NH3-TPD), reducibility of Cu oxide by temperature-programmed reduction (TPR), transmission electron microscope (TEM), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and copper surface area and particle size measurements by N2O titration method. Increasing the number of moderate acidic sites and facilitation of easily reducible copper species with small particle size are found to be the prime reasons for the superior functionality of the (NH4)2CO3 precipitated catalyst. The usage of (NH4)2CO3 also leaves no residual ions, whereas the presence of residual K+ and Na+ ions in the case of K2CO3 and Na2CO3 precipitated catalysts leads to lower activity and selectivity.
paragraphs: Biomass-derived H2-deficient and CO2-abundant syngas has been gaining more importance for the synthesis of methanol and dimethyl ether (DME), since these compounds are the most interesting renewable energy sources with high potential to minimize emissions of CO2 and NOx into the atmosphere and thereby reduce global warming. DME is an important ingredient for the production of a wide spectrum of chemicals such as dimethyl sulfate, methyl acetate and light olefins. DME is also considered to be environmentally benign to replace the harmful chlorofluorocarbons. The commercial process for the production of DME involves two steps; the first being synthesis of methanol by hydrogenation of CO and/or CO2 on Cu-ZnO-based catalysts and the second, production of DME by dehydration of methanol on solid-acid catalysts like γ-Al2O3 or modified ZSM-5 zeolite. Recently, a great emphasis has been laid on the development of a single-step process for the direct synthesis of DME using bifunctional catalysts that contain the above two functionalities.

The preparation of bifunctional catalysts is a complicated process and it needs special attention for proper control of active sites [6,12–14]. The redox and acidic properties of bifunctional catalysts have been observed to be influenced by several factors, such as precipitation at an optimum pH (∼7.0) and aging temperature (>70°C). Preparation of highly dispersed fine crystallites with high surface area of skeletal Cu by changing the conditions of precipitation, stabilization of active Cu species by adding promoters, modification of surface acidity of solid-acid catalyst by adding Na, Fe or Mg to ZSM-5 and by changing the silica-to-alumina ratio on silica-alumina support are some of the important variables to achieve highly active and selective catalysts.

The modification of surface acidity is the key variable to enhance the DME selectivity and for the prevention of further dehydration of DME to undesired hydrocarbons. In our previous investigation, a superior catalytic performance was demonstrated on Zr-modified ferrierite bifunctional catalyst in terms of high CO conversion and DME selectivity compared to the ZSM-5 and Y zeolite based catalysts, owing to the easy reducibility of metal component and the presence of proper acid site density that existed on the former. The superiority of ferrierite also lies in its favorable topology facilitating easy diffusion of the reactants and product molecules. Many works have been reported on the role and acidity of solid-acid component in the bifunctional catalysts. However, the information is scarce on the role and nature of precipitants such as Na2CO3, K2CO3 and (NH4)2CO3 on the catalytic properties of Zr-modified ferrierite and its implications on the conversion of biomass-derived H2-deficient and CO2-abundant syngas to methanol and DME.

Thus, the present investigation is focused on understanding the influence of the nature of precipitant used in the preparation on the physico-chemical properties and in turn, on their CO conversion activity and DME selectivity from biomass-derived model synthesis gas. The superiority of (NH4)2CO3 as a precipitant over Na2CO3 and K2CO3 has been demonstrated. The properties of the catalysts as measured by various methods such as nitrogen adsorption, temperature-programmed desorption of ammonia (NH3-TPD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscope (TEM), temperature-programmed reduction (TPR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and the measurements of metallic copper surface area are used to substantiate the arguments.

The Cu-ZnO-Al2O3/Zr-ferrierite bifunctional catalyst consisting 7:3 ratio of Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 component (for methanol synthesis) and Zr-ferrierite component (for DME synthesis) was prepared by a co-precipitation–deposition method. For the synthesis of Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 (component I) a metal oxide composition of 50wt.% CuO, 40wt.% ZnO and 10wt.% Al2O3 was chosen based on our previous studies. A mass of 5.03g of copper acetate monohydrate, 4.31g of zinc acetate dihydrate and 2.94g of aluminum nitrate were dissolved in 600mL of de-ionized water. The pH of mixed metal salt solution was found to be 5.5. Separate aqueous solutions of the precipitants were prepared for the precipitation. For example, a solution of sodium carbonate was made by dissolving 8.34g in 600mL of de-ionized water to get the pH in the range of 10.5–11.0.

The acidic component of Zr-ferrierite (component II) was prepared by loading 3wt.% of Zr (ZrCl2O·8H2O) on the ferrierite (Si/Al=25 provided by Zeolyst) by incipient wetness impregnation method. The final bifunctional catalyst was prepared by co-precipitation of component I in the slurry of component II, according to the procedure described below. The required quantity of previously synthesized Zr-ferrierite powder was added to 200mL of de-ionized water in a 2-L flask while stirring at around 70°C. Then the mixed metal precursor solution containing copper acetate, zinc acetate and aluminum nitrate was added to the slurry of Zr-ferrierite powder by using syringe pumps for precise control of the feeding rate with the addition of sodium carbonate solution simultaneously. The temperature of the mixture was maintained at 70°C during the precipitation and the pH measured after precipitation was found to be in the range of 7.5–8.0. The slurry obtained was further digested at 70°C for 3h. The precipitates were filtered, washed with 2000ml of hot de-ionized water and extruded to the size of ∼2mm in length and ∼1mm in thickness followed by drying for 16h at room temperature. The sample was further dried in an oven at 110°C for 12h and subsequently calcined at 350°C for 5h in air.

The catalysts are denoted as CZA-ZrFER(X), where CZA stands for the Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 component, ZrFER for the Zr-modified ferrierite zeolite. The X in the bracket denotes the alkali metal ion Na, K or NH3 ion for which Na2CO3, K2CO3 or (NH4)2CO3, is used as the precipitant.

The surface area and pore volume measurements were conducted by nitrogen adsorption and desorption isotherms obtained at −196°C using a constant-volume adsorption apparatus (Micromeritics, ASAP-2400). The pore volume was determined at a relative pressure (P/P o) of 0.99. The calcined samples were degassed at 250°C with a He flow for 4h before the measurements. The pore size distribution of samples was determined by the BJH (Barett–Joyner–Halenda) model from the desorption branch of the nitrogen isotherm.

The bifunctional catalysts were thoroughly characterized for their properties such as structural identification and crystallinity by the powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Rigaku diffractometer using Cu-Kα radiation), scanning electron microscopy (SEM; JEOL (JSM6700F)) for the morphology and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) for the surface composition. The morphology of bifunctional catalyst was also characterized by using the transmission electron microscopy (TEM; TECNAI G2 instrument).

The Cu metal area was measured by N2O surface titration method by using the home-made apparatus. Prior to the titration, the samples were reduced at 250°C for 4h with 5%H2/N2 flow, followed by purging and cooling with a He flow to 100°C. The consumption of N2O as well as the evolution of N2 on the metallic Cu sites (N2O+2Cu=Cu2O+N2) was measured by a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The surface area of metallic Cu was calculated by assuming 1.46×1019 Cuatoms/m2 and a N2O/Cus (Cu atom on surface) molar stoichiometry of 0.5 and the particle size of Cu was calculated with the equation of 6000/(8.92×Cu metal surface area/Cu fraction in gram catalyst) according to the previously reported work by Evans et al..

For the temperature-programmed reduction carried out on the BEL-CAT instrument, the samples were previously treated in He flow up to 350°C and kept for 2h to remove adsorbed water and other contaminants followed by cooling to 50°C. The 5%H2/He mixture was passed over the samples at a flow rate of 30mL/min with a heating rate of 10°C/min up to 500°C. The effluent gas was passed over a molecular sieve trap to remove the generated water and then analyzed by GC equipped with TCD.

The NH3-TPD experiments (Micromeritics, Autochem 2920) were performed to determine the surface acidity of calcined and used catalysts. About 0.1g of the sample was flushed initially with a He flow at 250°C for 2h, cooled to 100°C and saturated with NH3. Purging the sample with He flow was continued until equilibrium, and then TPD was carried out from 100 to 600°C at a heating rate of 10°C/min.

The surface electronic state of copper and zinc species after reaction for 16h were characterized by using the XPS (ESCALAB MK-II). During the experiments, the AlKα monochromatized line (1486.6eV) was adopted and the vacuum level was around 10−7 Pa. The used samples were previously pressed to thin pallet and the binding energies (BE) were corrected by adjusting with the reference BE of C1s (285.0eV).

The catalytic activity experiments were conducted in a fixed-bed stainless-steel reactor with a diameter of 12.7mm using 1.0g of the bifunctional catalyst. Prior to activity test, all the catalysts were reduced in 5% H2/N2 flow at 250°C for 4h under atmospheric pressure. The following reaction conditions were employed during activity test; T =250°C; P =4MPa; space velocity (SV)=5500L/kgcat/h and the molar feed composition of CO/CO2/H2 =41/21/38 (biomass-derived model synthesis gas). The effluent products were analyzed by an online GC (DS6200, Donam Co.) equipped with two columns; Porapack-Q connected to a TCD for non-flammable products (CO, CO2) and GS-Q to a flame ionization detector (FID) for flammable products such as methanol, DME and hydrocarbon byproducts. The CO conversion and product selectivities were calculated based on the total carbon balance. The average values obtained at a stable activity performance after 14–16h on stream were considered to evaluate the differences in catalytic activity.

The main reactions involved in DME synthesis from syngas are represented by the following reactions: (1) Methanol synthesis: CO+2H2 =CH3OH,ΔH°=−90.6kJ/mol (2) Methanol dehydration: 2CH3OH=CH3OCH3 +H2O,ΔH°=−23.4kJ/mol (3) WGS reaction: H2O+CO=H2 +CO2,ΔH°=−41.2kJ/mol (4) Net reaction: 3CO+3H2 =CH3OCH3 +CO2,ΔH°=−245.8kJ/mol

The enthalpy values indicate that the formation of DME (Eq. (4)) is thermodynamically more favorable compared to the other products (Eqs. (1)–(3)). The main advantage of the direct synthetic route to DME lies in surpassing the equilibrium constraint involved in methanol synthesis. The extra hydrogen generated through in situ water–gas shift (WGS) reaction (Eq. (3)) creates a hydrogen-rich reaction environment which is suitable for the higher conversions of CO. Thus, the conversion of CO is much higher in DME synthesis than in methanol synthesis, and the conversion and product distribution is altered according to the extent of WGS activity. Overall, these studies indicate that the production of methanol and DME are mainly controlled by kinetics rather than thermodynamics at CO2-rich and H2-deficient reaction conditions.

The bifunctional catalysts with varying catalytic properties are expected to exhibit different product patterns. The time on stream analysis displayed in Fig. 1 indicates the stable performance of all the catalysts studied over a period of 16h. The CO conversion activity realized is the highest in the case of CZA-ZrFER(NH3). A activity increase from 40.8% on CZA-ZrFER(K) to 59.4% on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) is observed. The data presented in Table 1 are the steady-state values of conversion and selectivity towards the desired products after a time on stream of 14h. Here again, the superiority of CZA-ZrFER(NH3) is apparent in terms of providing the highest DME selectivity. Interestingly, the highest DME selectivity is always accompanied by the highest CO conversion on these catalysts. This observation is indeed in accordance with the basic equations of DME synthesis. Although the amount of extra hydrogen produced by WGS reaction will be almost the same and the rate of methanol formation did not differ much, the faster consumption of methanol by dehydration is attributable to the higher CO conversion and DME selectivity. All the catalysts show an equilibrium selectivity of around 34% to CO2 due to the fast reaction rate of WGS reaction. The CO2 concentration in the product also reveals that the excess CO2 formed on these catalysts is not able to undergo hydrogenation to produce methanol or DME at the present reaction conditions of low H2 concentration. The reasons for the superior performance of CZA-ZrFER(NH3) have been examined with the help of several characterization techniques and the results are given below.

The pore size distribution patterns are displayed in Fig. 2 . The peak representing the population of pores with an average diameter shifts to the lower side. The sharpness of the peak is also increased suggesting a relatively narrow range distribution of pores in these catalysts. A progressive decrease in the average pore size (Table 2 ) occurs in the order of the precipitating agent: (NH4)2CO3 <K2CO3 <Na2CO3. The lowest pore diameter of 12.8nm is observed for the CZA-ZrFER(NH3) catalyst. Although the larger average pore diameter is generally beneficial for obtaining high catalytic activity by facile mass-transfer of reactants and products, the acid site density and reducibility of copper should be considered on bifunctional catalyst to elucidate the activity variation. The large pore above 10nm in size on bifunctional catalyst is mainly arising from the intra-grain structures of CZA components during co-precipitation step, and the micropore volume around 4nm (inserted figure in Fig. 2) is due to contribution from the ferrierite. The micropore volume which is related to the weak acid site density from ferrierite, is abundant on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) compared to others. This is suggesting that CZA components are evenly distributed at the outer surface of Zr-modified ferrierite on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) catalyst and the high DME selectivity is mainly attributed to these acid site density and reducibility of copper oxide that is crucial for methanol synthesis step.

The X-ray diffraction patterns of the calcined catalysts reveal structural integrity of ferrierite (particularly with the appearance of peaks below 2θ =30°) in all of them (Fig. 3 ). The appearance of peaks at 2θ =35.6° and 38.7° suggest the presence of well-dispersed CuO species. The extent of line broadening of the diffraction peak related to CuO particle (full width at half maximum (FWHM) value) increased on CZA-ZrFER(NH3), suggesting the formation of smaller Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 particles in this catalysts when compared to those on CZA-ZrFER(Na) and CZA-ZrFER(K).

The SEM images of the catalysts also exhibit different morphologies for different precipitants (Fig. 4 ). The average particle size of the bifunctional catalyst is larger when (NH4)2CO3 is used as a precipitant and smaller with K2CO3. The results reveal the presence of well-developed mesopores on the large plate-type particles representing the deposition of a nano-sized granule-type Cu-Zn-Al2O3 on ferrierite in CZA-ZrFER(NH3) catalyst, which is responsible for its larger surface area.

The TPR profiles of the catalysts are shown in Fig. 5 . The Cu reduction peak is shifted to lower temperature (from 246 to 230°C) as the precipitant changes from Na2CO3 to (NH4)2CO3 with an intermediate value for the catalyst prepared using K2CO3. A considerable decrease in the reduction temperature with CZA-ZrFER(NH3) catalyst implies formation of a more easily reducible Cu species. In the case of CZA-ZrFER(K), however, another shoulder peak at a higher temperature of 287°C is observed indicating that the complete reduction of the Cu species is rather difficult compared to that of the other two catalysts.

Acidity is another important factor that influences catalytic activity. The NH3-TPD patterns obtained on the catalysts are shown in Fig. 6 . The peaks were deconvoluted assuming Gaussian distribution and integrated at the maximum peak positions of T1, T2 and T3. The desorption peak T1 at ∼200°C is a characteristic peak for weak acidic site of ferrierite. This assignment has been confirmed by obtaining an NH3-TPD pattern on ZrFER sample. It can be seen from the figure that the weak acidity of the support is greatly diminished presumably by the presence of the alkali ion coming from the precipitant. Another peak T2 (medium acidic site), with its maximum at ∼320°C is observed on all the bifunctional catalysts representing the presence of acidic sites of medium strength. It is interesting to observe that this peak is highly intense for CZA-ZrFER(NH3) and weak in the case of catalysts prepared using Na2CO3 and K2CO3. Furthermore, all the catalysts exhibit a third prominent high temperature peak T3 (strong acidic site) at round 480°C. A quantitative comparison of three types of acidity calculated for all the samples is made in Table 3 . The acidity behavior of the catalysts is explained in detailed in the following paragraphs, based on the residual ions present in these catalysts.

An EDS analysis conducted on the freshly prepared samples of the bifunctional catalysts revealed that the residue content was 5.32wt.% Na on CZA-ZrFER(Na) and 1.38wt.% K on CZA-ZrFER(K), substantiating their role in altering the acidity. The residues can be either deposited on Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 component and/or ion-exchanged with acidic sites on Zr-modified ferrierite. Enough care was taken in the present study, thorough filtering and washing steps, to bring down the metal residue content to below 0.01wt.%. Therefore, the metal ions are expected to occupy ion-exchange positions (acidic surface) of ferrierite preferentially rather than their interaction with Cu-ZnO-Al2O3.

Among the three precipitants, (NH4)2CO3 is a good candidate for not leaving any metal residue on the catalyst surface. However, there could be a metal leaching problem during precipitation, as (NH4)2CO3 can form a soluble complex by reacting with Cu2+ and NH4+. Enough care has been taken in the present study to avoid metal leaching as well. While precipitating Cu, Zn and Al precursors with (NH4)2CO3 in the slurry of solid-acid component, the generated stable metal-ammonia complex was impregnated on the surface of Zr-modified ferrierite so as to reduce the leaching problem. Another advantage of this method lies in a slow release of ammonia from the decomposition of ammonium complex during calcination that can facilitate the formation of CZA-ZrFER(NH3) with narrow pore size distribution and high surface area.

The highest value of metallic surface area (Table 4 ) is observed for CZA-ZrFER(NH3), which is almost three times that of the other bifunctional catalysts, due to the presence of well-dispersed Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 particles formed in this catalyst and their facile reducibility at low temperature. The other two bifunctional catalysts CZA-ZrFER(Na) and CZA-ZrFER(K) exhibited lower values of metallic surface area due to the possible occurrence of the residual ion induced sintering of Cu metal during the calcination and reduction steps.

It is known that medium acidity catalyzes the DME formation whereas strong acidity enhances the formation of undesired hydrocarbons and coke precursors. Although the BET surface area and average pore diameter of bifunctional catalyst significantly changed with the precipitating agents, due to the variation of intra-grain structures of CZA components, the acidity was also varied. In the present study, the residual ions generated from the precipitating agents greatly influenced the acidic properties of the bifunctional catalysts. The desorption peak T1 is a characteristic peak for weak acidic site of ferrierite and the remaining peaks (T2 and T3) are attributed to the CZA component present on the surface of ferrierite. Therefore, the total acidic site density increased after CZA component addition to Zr-modified ferrierite from 1.491 up to 3.130mmol/g with the simultaneous decrease of weak acidic site (T1). In the present study, two peaks of T1 and T2 could be assigned to the active site for methanol dehydration, even though its too strong acidic strength is responsible for methanol reforming to CO2. Among the three precipitating agents, the catalyst prepared by using K2CO3 (Table 3) has the lowest value for weak and medium acidity (0.979mmol/g) which is the summation of the T1 and T2 acidity in Fig. 6, whereas that from (NH4)2CO3 shows the highest (2.181mmol/g) value. The CZA-ZrFER(NH3) also shows the highest number of total acidic sites. The reason for CZA-ZrFER(NH3) to exhibit the highest activity can be ascribed mainly to its capacity to retain larger quantity of the weak and medium acidity. The use of (NH4)2CO3 as a precipitant also helps in creating highly dispersed copper species on the surface as revealed by XRD, facilitating the formation of well-developed mesopores inside the nano size Cu-Zn-Al2O3 particles as seen in SEM and finally enhancing the reducibility of Cu oxide as observed in the TPR patterns, apart from enhancing the medium acidity. The CZA-ZrFER(K) possesses the characteristic strong acidic sites and difficultly reducible (Fig. 5 and Table 3) copper oxide species. Hence, the catalytic activity expressed in terms of CO conversion varied in the order CZA-ZrFER(NH3)>CZA-ZrFER(Na)>CZA-ZrFER(K). It is well reported that the catalytic activity is a strong function of copper metal area. However, a close look at the data given in Table 4 reveals that the metal surface area of the fresh catalysts varied in the order CZA-ZrFER(NH3)>CZA-ZrFER(K)>CZA-ZrFER(Na). In order to understand the reason for this discrepancy the catalysts collected after the reaction were subjected to further characterization.

All the used bifunctional catalysts exhibited decrease in strong acidity as well as total acidity after the reaction as shown in Table 3. However, the weak and medium acidic site density is still higher in the case of CZA-ZrFER(NH3). Interestingly, the medium acidity (T2) increased in all bifunctional catalysts after reaction with a decrease of strong acidity. The copper metal area of the used catalysts is now observed to be in the order CZA-ZrFER(NH3)>CZA-ZrFER(Na)>CZA-ZrFER(K). A substantial decrease in the metal area is also detected in all the catalysts. This implies that the catalysts undergo redistribution of the particle size of CZA components during the reaction with a possibility for sintering, the degree of which depending upon the nature of the precipitant used. The initial rate for CO2 and methanol formation is higher in all bifunctional catalysts with low DME selectivity until 2h on stream. Therefore, these variations such as decreased acidity and surface area of metallic copper could occur at the very beginning of reaction before 2h on stream. Table 4 provides the data on Cu metal particle sizes on catalysts analyzed before and after reaction. The particle size of Cu was calculated by using the equation of 6000/(8.92×Cu metal surface area/Cu fraction in gram catalyst). The particle size of the used catalysts varied in the order CZA-ZrFER(NH3)<CZA-ZrFER(Na)<CZA-ZrFER(K) which is consistent with the variation in the steady-state activity inversely, as displayed in Table 1 and Fig. 1. The small particle size on ZrFER and the high metallic surface area of copper is important to obtain a high catalytic performance. The morphology of used bifunctional catalysts is also observed by using the TEM analysis as shown in Fig. 7 . The CZA-ZrFER(Na) and CZA-ZrFER(K) show sphere-type granules of (Cu-ZnO-Al2O3), with size above ∼40nm, distributed on ZrFER. The Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 particles on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) are rod-type with diameter much smaller than the other catalysts. Interestingly, the trend of particle size variation is similar with the results of N2O titration. These small Cu-ZnO-Al2O3 particles on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) are attributed to the high catalytic activity due to facile reducibility.

The Cu2p/3/2 and Zn2p3/2 photoelectron spectra on the used bifunctional catalysts are shown in Fig. 8 . The BE of Cu2p/3/2 around 930eV is generally assigned to Cu+ and that around 933.5eV for Cu2+ with the characteristic satellite peaks between 940 and 945eV due to the electron shake-up process. The synergy effect on methanol synthesis could be obtained by the co-presence of two-dimensional Cu0-Cu+ layer which is causing a strong adsorption of CO instead of dissociative adsorption of CO (not active for methanol synthesis). All our bifunctional catalysts showed a distinctive BE of Cu2p/3/2 around 932–934eV and it suggests the co-presence of Cu0-Cu+ layer. The shift to lower BE of Cu2p/3/2 on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) compared to CZA-ZrFER(K) further suggests a well-dispersed two-dimensional Cu0-Cu+ layer which is active for methanol synthesis. In addition to the BE investigation, the experimental electron intensity ratio for Cu and Zn (I Cu/I Zn) could also correlated with copper particle size which was well established by many researchers. With the increase of I Cu/I Zn ratio, the particle size of copper decreases with the assumption of monolayer coverage of copper species or large particle formation with high blockage of the surface of support. The values of I Cu/I Zn ratio (Table 4) is 0.68, 0.51 and 0.92 for CZA-ZrFER(Na), CZA-ZrFER(K) and CZA-ZrFER(NH3), respectively. The higher value of I Cu/I Zn on CZA-ZrFER(NH3) suggests a small copper particle size formation with well-dispersed two-dimensional Cu0-Cu+ layer with low BE. These findings are well consistent with the results of N2O titration, TEM images and XRD analysis. Thus, even after undergoing considerable change in the particle size, the CZA-ZrFER(NH3) catalyst emerges as the best among the three catalysts.

The CZA-ZrFER bifunctional catalysts show stable activity in the direct synthesis of DME from biomass-derived syngas. The catalyst prepared using (NH4)2CO3 as the precipitant displays the best CO conversion and DME selectivity compared to the catalysts prepared using other precipitants. Generation of high BET surface area as well as the copper metal surface area, the presence of more number of weak and medium strength acid sites without presence of residual metal ions from precipitant and the easily reducible copper species with high dispersion are the prime reasons for the superior performance of the catalyst prepared using (NH4)2CO3.
